content.title: About
content.content: Beans and rice with meat is a classic dish that combines protein‑rich beans, carbohydrate‑dense rice, and lean meat (usually beef or pork). It provides a balanced nutrient profile, offers lasting satiety, and works well for lunch or dinner.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The bean‑grain combination supplies a complete amino‑acid profile, making the meal a full protein source.
In different countries the dish has local names: in Latin America it’s “arroz con frijoles”, in Spain “fabada con arroz”.
Traditionally beans are soaked overnight to reduce cooking time and improve digestibility.
Meat is often browned with onion and spices first, which deepens the flavor.
The dish is commonly garnished with fresh herbs, lime, or chili sauce for extra zest.

items.title: Rich plant protein
items.content: Beans provide about 21 g of protein per 100 g, making them an excellent protein source for vegetarians, and when paired with meat they form a complete protein.

items.title: Complex carbohydrates
items.content: Rice delivers slow‑releasing energy, helping maintain stable blood‑sugar levels.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Both meat and beans are high in vitamin B6, niacin, and folate, which are essential for metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: The meal supplies iron, zinc, magnesium, and potassium, supporting heart and muscle function.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Beans and whole‑grain rice provide fiber that promotes healthy digestion.

items.title: Digestive issues
items.content: Some people experience gas from beans; thorough rinsing and soaking can lessen this effect.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: If the recipe includes soy sauce or added salt, sodium levels can be high; monitor salt usage.

items.title: Bean allergy
items.content: Rarely, individuals may be allergic to beans; discontinue use if any reaction occurs.

items.title: Meat quality
items.content: Use fresh, reputable cuts of meat to avoid food‑borne illness.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Soak beans for 8–12 hours, then boil until tender. Cook rice separately. Sauté meat with onion, garlic, and spices (paprika, cumin, black pepper). Combine beans, rice, and meat, add broth, and simmer 15–20 minutes until flavors meld. Serve hot, garnished with fresh herbs.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the cooked dish in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. It can be frozen for up to 2 months; thaw in the fridge and reheat before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: A Bologna sandwich on wheat bread is a classic sandwich made with slices of cooked Bologna sausage, fresh vegetables, and sauce, placed between two slices of whole‑grain wheat bread. It is popular in Europe and the United States as a quick snack or light meal.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Bologna sausage gets its name from the Italian city of Bologna, where it is traditionally made from beef, pork and spices.
The first recorded recipe for a sandwich with Bologna dates back to early 19th‑century cookbooks.
Wheat bread provides a slower release of carbohydrates, keeping energy levels steadier than white bread.
The sandwich is often served with mustard or mayonnaise, lettuce, tomato and cucumber.
In some regions cheese such as Emmental or Cheddar is added for extra flavor.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Bologna provides about 12 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: Source of iron
items.content: Meat supplies heme iron, which is more readily absorbed than plant‑based iron.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Vitamins B1, B6 and B12 aid metabolism and support the nervous system.

items.title: Dietary fiber from whole‑grain bread
items.content: Whole‑grain wheat bread adds fiber that promotes digestive health.

items.title: Antioxidant content
items.content: Vitamin E present in the fat used for the sausage helps protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: High sodium
items.content: Processed meats often contain a lot of salt, which can raise blood pressure if consumed in excess.

items.title: Nitrites and preservatives
items.content: Nitrites are used to preserve color and shelf life; large amounts are considered potentially harmful.

items.title: Meat allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to components of the sausage.

items.title: Calorie dense
items.content: A sandwich can contain 300–450 kcal, so portion control is advisable for weight‑management diets.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Assemble the sandwich by layering slices of Bologna, lettuce, thinly sliced tomato and cucumber between two pieces of whole‑grain wheat bread. Add mustard, mayo or a yogurt‑based sauce if desired. It can be eaten by hand or cut into smaller pieces for children.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared sandwich refrigerated at 0–4 °C and consume within 24 hours. Store the sausage in its original packaging or an airtight container, and keep the bread in a dry place or sealed bag to prevent drying out.

content.title: About
content.content: Caesar salad with romaine is a classic dish composed of crisp romaine lettuce leaves, Parmesan cheese, croutons, and traditionally a dressing made from egg yolk, olive oil, anchovies, garlic, and lemon juice. In this version the dressing is omitted, allowing the natural bitterness and subtle sweetness of the lettuce to shine.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The salad was created in the 1920s at the Tijuana restaurant “Caesar’s” for American diplomat Caesar Cardini.
Romaine lettuce is rich in vitamins A and K as well as folate.
Traditional Caesar dressing often contains raw eggs, so many recipes use pasteurized alternatives for safety.
Croutons add a crunchy texture and help hold a small amount of dressing when it is used.
A dressing‑free version is popular among those watching calories and wanting to highlight the vegetables’ natural flavor.

items.title: Rich in vitamins A and K
items.content: Romaine provides carotenoids and vitamin K, supporting vision, immunity, and blood clotting.

items.title: Low‑calorie
items.content: Without dressing the salad contains about 15 kcal per 100 g, making it an excellent diet choice.

items.title: Source of fiber
items.content: Dietary fiber aids digestion and promotes satiety.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Phytonutrients in romaine help combat free radicals.

items.title: Supports bone health
items.content: Vitamin K and calcium in the leaves contribute to strong bones.

items.title: Leaf contamination
items.content: Salad greens can be contaminated with bacteria (E. coli, Salmonella); thorough washing is essential.

items.title: Parmesan allergy
items.content: People sensitive to dairy may react to the cheese.

items.title: High oxalate content
items.content: For individuals prone to kidney stones, excessive oxalates may be a concern.

items.title: Digestive discomfort in large portions
items.content: Eating a lot of raw greens can cause gas in sensitive individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the salad cold, laying romaine leaves on a plate, sprinkling grated Parmesan and crunchy croutons on top. Optional additions include grilled chicken, shrimp, or tofu for extra protein.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep lettuce in the refrigerator in a perforated bag or container with a paper towel to absorb excess moisture. Use within 1‑2 days, as leaves become limp after that.

content.title: About
content.content: Coleslaw dressing is a creamy blend of mayonnaise, sour cream, vinegar, and spices designed to coat finely shredded cabbage, carrots, and other vegetables. It gives the dish a smooth, slightly tangy flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Coleslaw originated in the United States and became popular in the mid‑19th century.
The dressing often contains mustard, which enhances aroma and helps emulsify the mixture.
There are many variations, from classic creamy to lighter yogurt‑based versions.
Some recipes add apple cider vinegar for extra zest.
Coleslaw is commonly served as a side to barbecue, sandwiches, and fried foods.

items.title: Source of vitamin C
items.content: The vegetables in coleslaw, such as cabbage and carrots, are rich in vitamin C, which supports the immune system.

items.title: Probiotic content (when using yogurt)
items.content: Yogurt‑based dressing contains live cultures that promote gut health.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Beta‑carotene from carrots and other phytochemicals help combat free radicals.

items.title: Low in added sugar
items.content: Unlike many sauces, classic coleslaw dressing does not contain added sugars.

items.title: Aids digestion
items.content: The acidity of vinegar stimulates stomach acid production, improving digestion.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: The dressing often contains mayonnaise and sour cream, which can trigger reactions in people with lactose intolerance or milk allergy.

items.title: High fat content
items.content: The creamy base makes the dressing calorie‑dense; portion control is recommended.

items.title: Raw egg content (in mayonnaise)
items.content: Traditional mayonnaise may contain raw eggs, posing a salmonella risk for vulnerable groups.

items.title: Sodium
items.content: Many dressings are salty; those with hypertension should choose low‑salt versions.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Toss the dressing with thinly shredded cabbage, carrots, radish, and onion. Mix well and let it rest for 15–30 minutes for flavors to meld. It can also be used as a sandwich spread, in wraps, or as a dip for vegetable sticks.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the dressing in a sealed container in the refrigerator at 0 °C–4 °C. Once opened, it is best used within 5–7 days. Discard if you notice off‑smell, color change, or mold.

content.title: About
content.content: A doughnut is a small sweet fried or baked pastry, often topped with chocolate icing. The batter is usually made from wheat flour, eggs, milk, sugar and yeast, and after cooking it is coated with a smooth chocolate glaze, sometimes sprinkled with nuts or sprinkles.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Doughnuts originated in Europe in the 19th century and quickly became popular in the United States.
The classic American doughnut has a ring shape, while in Russia and many other countries doughnuts are often without a hole.
Chocolate icing may contain cocoa butter, powdered sugar and butter, giving it a glossy and creamy texture.
In some countries doughnuts are filled with jam, custard, cream or fruit puree.
Doughnuts are often associated with holidays – for example, they are a traditional treat on Thanksgiving in the US.

items.title: Quick energy source
items.content: Doughnuts provide fast‑acting carbohydrates and sugar, making them a convenient quick snack.

items.title: Iron content
items.content: When made with whole‑grain flour, doughnuts can contain modest amounts of iron, which supports blood formation.

items.title: Calcium from dairy
items.content: Milk and butter in the batter supply calcium, essential for bone health.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Large amounts of sugar can contribute to weight gain and increase the risk of dental caries.

items.title: Trans and saturated fats
items.content: Frying in oil can add trans‑fats and saturated fats, which are unfavorable for cardiovascular health.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Traditional doughnut batter contains wheat flour, making it unsuitable for people with celiac disease.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy doughnuts in moderation as a dessert or quick snack. They pair well with coffee, tea or milk. For extra indulgence, split them and add whipped cream or fruit sauce.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store doughnuts in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 2‑3 days. For longer shelf life, keep them in the refrigerator, where they stay fresh for about a week but may become less soft.

funnel-cake-with-sugar-and-fruit.title: Funnel Cake with Sugar and Fruit

content.title: About
content.content: Funnel cake is a deep‑fried batter formed into a lacy net, dusted with sugar and served with a variety of fresh fruits. The batter is typically made from flour, eggs, milk, sugar and leavening, then poured through a funnel into hot oil until golden and crisp. Sugar adds sweetness, while berries or sliced fruits bring aroma and a bright flavor contrast.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Funnel cake originated in the United States in the early 20th century and became a staple at fairs and festivals.
Traditionally the batter is poured through a funnel or squeeze bottle, creating the characteristic “mesh” pattern.
In Russia a similar treat is known as “testovoe oblako” or fried pancake‑net, but the authentic recipe retains its American roots.
Sugar is usually sprinkled immediately after frying while the cake is still hot, allowing it to melt slightly.
Common fruit toppings include strawberries, raspberries, kiwi, banana or lightly caramelized apples.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: The batter provides carbohydrates and a modest amount of protein, delivering quick energy.

items.title: Vitamins from fruit
items.content: Fresh berries and fruits are rich in vitamin C, vitamin A and antioxidants that support immunity.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: The cake contains potassium and magnesium, while fruit adds calcium and iron.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Fruit toppings increase fiber content, aiding digestion.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: Fresh fruit contributes water, helping maintain fluid balance.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Large amounts of sugar can raise blood glucose levels and contribute to tooth decay.

items.title: Fried oil
items.content: Deep‑frying adds saturated fats and calories, which should be consumed in moderation.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Traditional recipes use wheat flour, making it unsuitable for people with celiac disease.

items.title: Fruit allergies
items.content: Certain fruits may trigger allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the funnel cake hot, dusted with powdered sugar and topped with fresh berries, sliced banana, kiwi or other fruits. Eat it straight away with a fork or by hand, optionally drizzling light syrup or whipped cream.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Funnel cake is best enjoyed immediately after frying. Leftovers can be kept in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2 days and reheated in the oven to restore crispness. Freezing is not recommended, as the texture deteriorates.

content.title: About
content.content: Green peas are the edible seeds of the pea plant (Pisum sativum) harvested at full maturity and boiled. They have a mild, slightly sweet flavor and a tender yet slightly crisp texture. Peas are commonly served as a side dish, and used in salads, soups, and purees.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Green peas are a good source of plant protein.
They are cultivated in temperate regions worldwide.
Peas belong to the legume family, which can fix nitrogen in the soil.
Ancient cultures used peas both as food and medicine.
There are many varieties differing in pod size and seed color.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: One cup of cooked peas provides about 8 g of protein, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Dietary fiber aids digestion and promotes satiety.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Peas contain folate, thiamine, and vitamin B6, important for metabolism.

items.title: Mineral content
items.content: They provide iron, magnesium, phosphorus, and potassium, supporting heart and nerve function.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Peas raise blood sugar slowly, which is beneficial for glucose control.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience an allergic reaction to legumes.

items.title: Gas production
items.content: Legumes can cause flatulence in sensitive people.

items.title: Purine content
items.content: Large amounts may increase uric acid levels in people prone to gout.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Peas can be enjoyed as a standalone side, added to salads, soups, stews, mashed into puree, or incorporated into vegetable casseroles. They pair well with mint, lemon, garlic, and olive oil.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked peas in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. Frozen peas retain quality for up to 6 months.

ice-cream-vanilla-with-additional-ingred.title: Ice cream, vanilla, with additional ingredients

content.title: About
content.content: Vanilla ice cream is a classic dessert made from milk, cream, sugar and natural vanilla flavoring. In this version additional ingredients (such as nuts, chocolate chips, berries) are mixed into the base, enriching both taste and texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Vanilla is the most expensive spice in the world; its flavor comes from the seeds of the orchid Vanilla planifolia.
The first vanilla‑flavoured ice cream appeared in Europe in the 17th century.
Adding extra ingredients allows for more than 400 flavor variations, making ice cream a highly versatile dessert.
Vanilla ice cream is often used in culinary shows for “soft‑serve” effects because it molds easily.
Traditionally ice cream was served as a soft scoop, but modern techniques create rolls, sandwiches, and even milk‑shake‑style desserts.

items.title: Source of calcium
items.content: Dairy components provide calcium, essential for strong bones and teeth.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Cream and milk contain vitamin B12 and riboflavin, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Vanilla antioxidants
items.content: Vanilla contains vanillin, an antioxidant that helps combat free radicals.

items.title: Quick energy
items.content: The fat and sugar content offers a rapid source of energy when consumed in moderation.

items.title: Mood‑boosting effect
items.content: Sweet taste and creamy texture can improve mood by triggering endorphin release.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: Dairy ingredients may cause discomfort for people lacking lactase.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Excessive consumption can contribute to weight gain and elevated blood glucose.

items.title: Allergy to nuts or other add‑ins
items.content: If nuts, chocolate, or berries are included, allergic reactions are possible.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Ice cream is rich in fats and calories, so portion control is advisable.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Ice cream can be enjoyed with a spoon, as an ice‑cream sandwich, blended into smoothies, or used as a base for dessert sauces. Sprinkle extra ingredients (nuts, fruit, chocolate) just before serving to keep them crunchy.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store ice cream in a freezer at –18 °C (0 °F) or lower. After opening, use within 1–2 weeks to prevent ice crystal formation and flavor loss. Do not leave ice cream at room temperature for more than 30 minutes.

oatmeal-instant-plain-made-with-water-no.title: Instant Oatmeal, plain, made with water

content.title: About
content.content: Instant oatmeal consists of whole oat groats that have been steamed and cut into small flakes so they dissolve quickly in hot water. The product contains no added fat, sugar, or flavorings, providing a pure source of complex carbohydrates.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Oats are one of the oldest cultivated grains, grown for more than 5,000 years.
Instant oatmeal can be prepared in 1–2 minutes, making it popular with students and travelers.
Oats belong to the grass family and are close relatives of wheat and barley.
Oat flakes are used not only in food but also in cosmetics for scrubs and masks.
In the United States, over 30 % of the population eats oatmeal for breakfast regularly.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Both soluble and insoluble fiber improve digestion, promote satiety, and help regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Source of beta‑glucan
items.content: Beta‑glucan lowers LDL cholesterol and supports the immune system.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: B1, B5 and folate are involved in energy metabolism and nervous‑system health.

items.title: Minerals: iron and magnesium
items.content: Iron is essential for oxygen transport, while magnesium supports muscle and nerve function.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: The absence of added fat makes it suitable for calorie‑controlled diets.

items.title: Oat allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience allergic reactions to oats or oat proteins.

items.title: Gluten cross‑contamination
items.content: Oats are often processed on the same lines as wheat, so gluten contamination is possible.

items.title: Phytic acid
items.content: Phytates can reduce the absorption of certain minerals when consumed in large amounts.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pour 200 ml of boiling water over the oatmeal, stir, and let stand for 1–2 minutes. You can add berries, nuts, honey, or protein powder. Use less water for a thicker consistency.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place in a tightly sealed package. After opening, use within 1–2 weeks to prevent moisture absorption and loss of crisp texture.

content.title: About
content.content: Reduced‑sodium canned vegetable soup is a ready‑to‑eat product made from selected vegetables that are quickly cooked and sealed in an airtight can. The lower salt level makes it suitable for people watching their sodium intake.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The soup retains most of the vitamins and minerals thanks to rapid heat processing.
Metal cans provide a long shelf life without the need for added preservatives.
Sodium reduction is achieved by replacing part of the salt with natural herbs and spices.
Typical vegetables include carrots, celery, onion, and tomatoes, giving a bright flavor and color.
The product is convenient for travel and situations with limited access to fresh foods.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: The vegetable blend supplies vitamins B1, B2 and B6, which support energy metabolism.

items.title: Low sodium content
items.content: Reduced salt helps maintain normal blood pressure.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber promotes healthy digestion and contributes to satiety.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Lycopene and carotenoids from tomatoes and carrots act as antioxidants.

items.title: Convenient and quick to prepare
items.content: The soup is ready after a short heating, saving time.

items.title: Allergy to ingredients
items.content: Spices or flavorings used may trigger allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Presence of preservatives
items.content: Some versions may contain small amounts of preservatives to extend shelf life.

items.title: Contains monosodium glutamate
items.content: Certain formulations use MSG, which some people prefer to avoid.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Open the can, pour the soup into a pot and bring to a boil for 5‑7 minutes. Optionally garnish with fresh herbs, a splash of cream, or cooked rice.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the unopened can in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, keep refrigerated and consume within 3‑4 days.

toddler-formula-store-brand-pediatric-sh.title: Toddler formula, store brand, pediatric shake

content.title: About
content.content: The "Store Brand Pediatric Shake" toddler formula is designed for children aged 1 to 3 years. It is enriched with vitamins, minerals, and proteins essential for growth and development. The formula is produced under strict quality standards and is safe for daily consumption.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Developed in collaboration with pediatricians to provide a complete nutrient profile.
Contains DHA and ARA – fatty acids important for brain and eye development.
Free from artificial colors and flavors.
Each serving provides 20 % of the daily iron requirement, helping prevent anemia.
Packaged for 30 servings, convenient for refrigerator storage.

items.title: Supports bone growth
items.content: Includes calcium and vitamin D, which promote strong bone formation.

items.title: Brain development
items.content: DHA and ARA support neural connections and visual function.

items.title: Immune support
items.content: Vitamins A, C and zinc help maintain the body’s defense mechanisms.

items.title: Energy provision
items.content: Lactose and complex carbohydrates provide a steady energy supply throughout the day.

items.title: Digestive health
items.content: Probiotics in the formula support a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: The product contains milk protein; consult a physician if an allergy is suspected.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: Children with lactose intolerance may experience discomfort; consider a lactose‑free alternative.

items.title: Iron content
items.content: Excessive iron intake can cause constipation; follow the recommended dosage.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Mix one serving (30 g) with 150 ml of warm (not hot) water or breast milk. Stir thoroughly until smooth. The product is typically offered 2–3 times daily according to the child’s needs.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the package in a dry, cool place away from direct sunlight. After opening, keep refrigerated and use within 30 days. Discard if the packaging is damaged or the product has an off‑odor.
